source_refs.note: Topic 11.2, printed pages 238-245: arteries, capillaries, veins, regulation of capillary flow, vasoconstriction and vasodilation, the velocity of blood, and the pulmonary and systemic circulations with their coronary, hepatic portal and renal parts.

blocks.text: Arteries, veins and capillaries are the main blood vessels of the human circulatory system.

blocks.title: Blue babies
blocks.text: Some abnormal babies have blueness (cyanosis) of the skin: blue babies. It is due to the mixing of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood between the two atria, so mixed blood is supplied to the body. Cyanosis results from the failure of the interatrial foramen, a temporary opening in the embryonic heart between the right and left atria, to close during development; it may also result from the failure of the ductus arteriosus, a temporary channel between the embryonic pulmonary artery and aorta, to constrict fully.
Arteries

Arteries carry blood away from the heart to the different parts of the body; all carry oxygenated blood except the pulmonary arteries. The central core of an artery is the lumen, and its wall has three layers: the outer tunica externa or adventitia of connective and elastic tissue, the middle tunica media of thick muscular tissue and elastic fibres, and the inner tunica intima, a thin layer of endothelial cells. The middle layer is important because it can withstand the higher blood pressure of ventricular systole. Arteries divide into smaller vessels, arterioles, which divide repeatedly until they form a dense network of very fine branches, the capillaries.

blocks.alt: A cut-away artery shown as stepped cylinders: the lumen at the centre, lined by the tunica intima (endothelium); around it the tunica media of smooth muscles and elastic tissue; and outermost the thick tunica externa, with arterioles branching off.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.6: Structure of artery (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.6).

blocks.text: Capillaries

Capillaries are formed by the division of arterioles and join to form venules. They penetrate all tissues and reach the cellular level. Their walls are a single layer of endothelial cells and their internal diameter is about 8 micrometres. Capillaries are the sites where materials are exchanged between the blood and the body tissues by diffusion or active transport: water and diffusible substances pass through the capillary walls, through the endothelial cells or through the intercellular spaces, and some materials are taken up by the wall cells by endocytosis and passed to the other side by exocytosis. The pressure within the capillaries causes a continuous leakage of fluid from the plasma into the tissues; this interstitial fluid consists of water with dissolved nutrients, hormones, gases, wastes and small proteins. Large proteins, RBCs and platelets remain within the capillaries, but some WBCs can squeeze out through the intercellular spaces of the wall.

blocks.alt: A capillary as a narrow tube whose wall is a single layer of flat endothelial cells; at its open end a red blood cell fills most of the lumen.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.7: Structure of capillary (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.7).

blocks.title: How close and how long
blocks.text: No cell of the body is more than 100 micrometres from a capillary. Capillaries are so narrow that RBCs must pass through them in single file, and the total length of the capillaries of an adult is estimated at over 80,600 kilometres, enough to encircle the globe twice.
Veins

Veins carry blood from the different parts of the body towards the heart; all carry deoxygenated blood except the pulmonary veins. Their walls have the same three layers as arteries: the tunica externa of connective and elastic tissue, a tunica media that is relatively thin and only slightly muscular with few elastic fibres, and the tunica intima of endothelial cells. The middle layer is thinner than in arteries because veins do not have to withstand high blood pressure; an empty artery is still a hollow tube, but an empty vein collapses like an empty balloon. Semilunar valves in the veins prevent the backflow of blood as it moves towards the heart, and the pressure of the surrounding muscles as they contract presses the veins and assists the return of blood. Smaller veins join to form larger veins and ultimately the venae cavae (inferior and superior), which pour blood into the right atrium; the pulmonary veins from the lungs empty into the left atrium.

blocks.text: Regulation of blood flow in capillaries

The amount of blood flowing in the capillaries is controlled by constricting or dilating them: nervous stimulation can constrict capillaries and certain chemicals such as histamine can dilate them. Some capillaries are connected with the arterioles and venules through loops of other capillaries, and the entry of each loop is guarded by a ring of muscle, a precapillary sphincter, which regulates the amount of blood flowing through the capillaries.

blocks.alt: An arteriole across the top and a venule across the bottom, joined by six capillary loops that are red near the arteriole and blue near the venule. A ring-shaped pre-capillary sphincter sits where each loop leaves the arteriole.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.10: Pre-capillary sphincters (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.10).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Arteriole, Pre-capillary sphincter, Capillaries, Venule.

blocks.text: Vasoconstriction and vasodilation in arterioles

The walls of arterioles have more circular muscle than elastic tissue, and the contraction of these circular muscles is under the control of the nervous and endocrine systems. When the muscles contract the arterioles are constricted, in vasoconstriction, which reduces the flow of blood in them; when they relax the arterioles are dilated, in vasodilation, which increases the flow. Vasoconstriction and vasodilation happen in response to changes in the metabolic activity of tissues: when activity in a tissue rises, oxygen decreases and carbon dioxide increases in its interstitial fluid, the circular muscles of its arterioles relax (vasodilation), and the increased flow in the arterioles and capillaries supplies more oxygen and removes more carbon dioxide. Decreased metabolic activity similarly causes vasoconstriction of the arterioles.

blocks.alt: Two arterioles below a row of active tissue cells. Left: a narrow arteriole with normal blood flow into its capillaries; the tissue fluid above has more oxygen. Right: the tissue fluid has less oxygen and more carbon dioxide, and a wider, dilated arteriole carries increased blood flow into the capillaries.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.11: Vasodilation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.11).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Active tissue, Less oxygen, More carbon dioxide, Normal blood flow, Capillaries, Increased blood flow, dilated arteriole.

blocks.text: Rate of blood flow

The velocity of blood flow differs in different vessels. It is highest in the aorta (450 to 500 mm per second), falls along the network of arteries and arterioles, and is lowest in the capillaries (about 1 mm per second); it rises again in the venules, veins and venae cavae (250 to 300 mm per second). These changes in velocity result from changes in the total cross-section of the vessel system.

blocks.alt: A graph with velocity of blood flow (mm/sec) from 0 to 500 on the y-axis and coloured bands for aorta, arteries, arterioles, capillaries, venules, veins and vena cava along the x-axis. The yellow curve starts near 480 in the aorta, falls through the arteries and arterioles to almost zero in the capillaries, then rises through the venules and veins to about 270 in the vena cava.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.12: Velocity of blood, moving in different vessels (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.12).

blocks.text: Circulatory pathways

In humans, and in all mammals and birds, blood circulates in two main pathways: the pulmonary circulation, to and from the lungs, and the systemic circulation, to and from the other parts of the body.

blocks.alt: The heart in the centre. Pulmonary circulation: pulmonary arteries (blue) carry blood to capillary beds in the right and left lungs, and right and left pulmonary veins (red) return it. Systemic circulation: the aorta (red) carries blood up to the arms and head and down to the internal organs and legs; the superior and inferior venae cavae (blue) return it. Arrows show the direction of flow and brackets mark the two circulations.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.13: Pulmonary and systemic circulations (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.13).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Superior vena cava, Arms and head, Aorta, Pulmonary arteries, Right lung, Left lung, Right pulmonary vein, Left pulmonary vein, Internal organs, Inferior vena cava, Legs, Systemic circulation, Pulmonary circulation.

blocks.text: Pulmonary circulation

The pulmonary circulation supplies deoxygenated blood to the lungs and returns oxygenated blood to the heart. The pulmonary trunk, a big artery, carries deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle and divides into the right and left pulmonary arteries to the two lungs. Inside each lung the pulmonary artery divides into pulmonary arterioles and lung capillaries, where the blood is oxygenated. The lung capillaries join to form pulmonary venules, which join to form the pulmonary veins; the left and right pulmonary veins open into the left atrium.
Systemic circulation
The systemic circulation supplies oxygenated blood to all the cells, tissues and organs of the body except the lungs and returns deoxygenated blood to the heart. It has the following components.

items: Coronary circulation: the heart walls are supplied through a small portion of the systemic circulation. The right and left coronary arteries arise from the aorta near its origin and divide into smaller arteries, arterioles and capillaries. After supplying oxygenated blood to the heart muscle, the capillaries unite into venules that make many coronary veins, which join to form the coronary sinus opening into the right atrium; small coronary veins drain directly into the right atrium.

blocks.alt: Two views of the heart with the vena cava and aorta above. Anterior view: the left and right coronary arteries arise from the base of the aorta and branch over the heart wall, with coronary veins beside them. Posterior view: coronary veins run up into the large coronary sinus that crosses the back of the heart, with the right coronary artery beside it.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.14: Coronary circulation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.14).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Left coronary artery, Right coronary artery, Coronary veins, Coronary sinus, Right coronary artery, (Anterior view), (Posterior view).

items: Hepatic portal circulation: a portal system is a circulation in which veins end in capillaries. In the hepatic portal system a large hepatic portal vein collects blood from the spleen and alimentary canal and takes it to the liver, from which the hepatic veins carry it to the heart. The blood from the alimentary canal contains the substances absorbed from the small intestine, which pass through the liver before going to the heart; the liver removes harmful substances and absorbs nutrients for storage. The system extends from the lower part of the oesophagus to the upper part of the anal canal.

blocks.alt: The liver with the stomach, spleen and pancreas beside it, and the colon framing the small intestine below. Veins from the small intestine, colon, pancreas and spleen join into the hepatic portal vein, which enters the liver and branches there. Hepatic veins carry blood from the liver into the inferior vena cava, which runs up the middle.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.15: Hepatic portal system (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.15).
blocks.long_description: Labels: Inferior vena cava, Hepatic veins, Spleen, Pancreas, Hepatic portal vein, Ascending colon, Descending colon, Small intestine.

items: Renal circulation: the right and left renal arteries carry oxygenated blood to the kidneys. Inside the kidney each renal artery divides repeatedly into smaller arteries, which branch into several afferent arterioles supplying the nephrons (the units of the kidney). Each afferent arteriole divides into the capillaries of a glomerulus, which unite into an efferent arteriole; this divides into two sets of capillaries, the peritubular capillaries around the nephron tubule in the cortex and the vasa recta around the tubule in the medulla. These capillaries unite into venules, which converge into smaller veins and finally the renal vein.

blocks.alt: Left: a nephron with its blood supply. A smaller artery gives the afferent arteriole, which forms the glomerulus; the efferent arteriole leaves it and forms peri-tubular capillaries round the coiled tubule and vasa recta along the loop; a venule drains into a smaller vein. Right: a kidney in section with smaller arteries spreading from the renal artery, and the renal vein leaving it.
blocks.caption: Figure 11.16: Renal circulation (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 11.16, printed as 'Renal portal system').
